## What is the problem?

A price depends on expected cash-flows and on a risk premium. Expected
cash-flows are the money the asset is expected to pay. The risk premium
is the extra return an investor requires because those expected
cash-flows are risky.

In a discounted cash flow, the two objects come from different
models. One model forecasts the expected cash-flows. Another model
supplies the premium used to turn those expected cash-flows into a
price. The two models do not have to agree about when times are bad,
or about how expected cash-flows behave when times are bad.

## Why should the risk premium come from the same model as the cash-flows?

The risk premium is payment for the risk in the expected cash-flows.
It should depend on how expected cash-flows move when times are bad,
and on whether the investor already dislikes those times.

## What is the solution?

Use a general equilibrium asset pricing model. General equilibrium
here means that prices come from one economy and one investor. Every
asset is a claim on that economy. Expected cash-flows and the risk
premium then come from how much the asset's expected cash-flows move
with the economy. If that movement changes, both the expected
cash-flows and the extra return required to hold the asset change
with it.

The course builds one model of this kind and uses it to price claims,
including a claim you bring yourself.

Start with [two free numbers](chapters/01-two-free-numbers.qmd).
Then [price a claim of your own](chapters/11-price-your-own-claim.qmd).
